section.title: The Lost Sheep, Coin, and Son
section.sectionRationale: When the Pharisees grumble that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, He answers with three parables of things lost and found: a shepherd who leaves ninety-nine to seek one sheep, a woman who sweeps her house for one coin, and a father who runs to embrace a son who was dead and is alive again. Each ends in a celebration, and the last leaves an elder brother standing outside, unwilling to rejoice. This is the heart of the gospel: the joy of heaven over one sinner who repents.
section.thesis: Because heaven rejoices over one sinner who repents, God Himself seeks the lost until He finds them and runs to welcome the returning, so the only true response is to come home and to join the Father's joy, not to stand outside it like the elder son.
section.frameNote: Three parables in one movement: the lost sheep sought, the lost coin swept for, and the lost son welcomed home, closing with the father's plea to the elder brother.

units.label: The grumble and the lost sheep
units.note: joy in heaven over one who repents

verses.text: Now all the tax collectors and sinners were gathering around to listen to Jesus.
So the Pharisees and scribes began to grumble: “This man welcomes sinners and eats with them.”
Then Jesus told them this parable:
“What man among you, if he has a hundred sheep and loses one of them, does not leave the ninety-nine in the pasture and go after the one that is lost, until he finds it?
And when he finds it, he joyfully puts it on his shoulders,
comes home, and calls together his friends and neighbors to tell them, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost sheep!’
I tell you that in the same way there will be more {{chara|joy}} in heaven over one sinner who {{metanoeo|repents}} than over ninety-nine righteous ones who do not need to repent.

units.label: The lost coin
units.note: she searches carefully until she finds it

verses.text: Or what woman who has ten silver coins and loses one of them does not light a lamp, sweep her house, and search carefully until she finds it?
And when she finds it, she calls together her friends and neighbors to say, ‘Rejoice with me, for I have found my lost coin.’
In the same way, I tell you, there is joy in the presence of God’s angels over one sinner who repents.”

units.label: The lost son and the father's welcome
units.note: this son of mine was dead and is alive again

verses.text: Then Jesus said, “There was a man who had two sons.
The younger son said to him, ‘Father, give me my share of the estate.’ So he divided his property between them.
After a few days, the younger son got everything together and journeyed to a distant country, where he squandered his wealth in wild living.
After he had spent all he had, a severe famine swept through that country, and he began to be in need.
So he went and hired himself out to a citizen of that country, who sent him into his fields to feed the pigs.
He longed to fill his belly with the pods the pigs were eating, but no one would give him a thing.
Finally he came to his senses and said, ‘How many of my father’s hired servants have plenty of food, but here I am, starving to death!
I will get up and go back to my father and say to him, “Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you.
I am no longer worthy to be called your son. Make me like one of your hired servants.”’
So he got up and went to his father. But while he was still in the distance, his father saw him and was filled with {{splanchnizomai|compassion}}. He ran to his son, embraced him, and kissed him.
The son declared, ‘Father, I have sinned against heaven and against you. I am no longer worthy to be called your son.’
But the father said to his servants, ‘Quick! Bring the best robe and put it on him. Put a ring on his finger and sandals on his feet.
Bring the fattened calf and kill it. Let us feast and celebrate.
For this son of mine was dead and is alive again! He was {{apollymi|lost}} and is found!’ So they began to celebrate.
Meanwhile the older son was in the field, and as he approached the house, he heard music and dancing.
So he called one of the servants and asked what was going on.
‘Your brother has returned,’ he said, ‘and your father has killed the fattened calf, because he has him back safe and sound.’
The older son became angry and refused to go in. So his father came out and pleaded with him.
But he answered his father, ‘Look, all these years I have served you and never disobeyed a commandment of yours. Yet you never gave me even a young goat so I could celebrate with my friends.
But when this son of yours returns from squandering your wealth with prostitutes, you kill the fattened calf for him!’
‘Son, you are always with me,’ the father said, ‘and all that is mine is yours.
But it was fitting to celebrate and be glad, because this brother of yours was dead and is alive again; he was lost and is found.’”

chara.gloss: Joy, gladness. Each parable ends in joy: the shepherd rejoicing, the woman calling neighbors to rejoice, the father throwing a feast. Jesus lifts this joy to heaven itself, where God and His angels rejoice over one sinner who turns home. The grumbling of the Pharisees is answered by the rejoicing of God.

metanoeo.gloss: To repent, to change one's mind and turn around. The sheep is carried, the coin is swept up, and the son comes to his senses and returns; each pictures repentance as being found by God and coming home to Him. Heaven's joy is over one such sinner who repents.

splanchnizomai.gloss: To be moved with compassion from deep within, in the gut. While the son is still far off, the father is seized with this visceral compassion and runs, an undignified sprint of love. The word reveals the heart of God toward returning sinners: not cold permission but overflowing mercy.

apollymi.gloss: To lose, to be lost, to perish. The same word binds the three parables together: the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son. To be lost is to be perishing away from God; to be found is to be restored to life, was dead and is alive again.

basic.context: The tax collectors and sinners crowd around Jesus, and the religious leaders grumble that He welcomes such people and even eats with them. Jesus answers with three parables. A shepherd leaves ninety-nine sheep to find one that is lost and carries it home rejoicing. A woman lights a lamp and sweeps her whole house until she finds one lost coin, then calls her neighbors to celebrate. A father divides his estate, watches his younger son waste it all in a far country, and then, while the boy is still far off, runs to embrace him and throws a feast, for this son was dead and is alive again. But the elder son, dutiful and cold, refuses to come in, and the father pleads with him too.
basic.hermeneutics: Read the three as one answer to the grumble of verse 2. Heaven's joy over the found sinner is the thread. The first two parables stress God's active seeking; the third opens up the heart of the Father and turns the mirror on the grumblers themselves, pictured in the elder brother who will not share his father's joy.
basic.originalLanguages: The word chara, joy, crowns each parable and rises to heaven itself. To be found is to metanoeo, to repent, to come home. The father is moved with splanchnizomai, gut-deep compassion, and runs. And the refrain that binds all three is apollymi, lost: the lost sheep, the lost coin, the lost son, each restored to life.
basic.typology: The seeking shepherd fulfills God's promise in Ezekiel to search for His scattered sheep Himself. The father who runs and clothes his son foreshadows the God who covers the shame of returning sinners. The feast over the found son points to the joy of the kingdom's table and the marriage supper of the Lamb.
basic.christ: Jesus is the shepherd who goes after the one lost sheep and lays it on His shoulders, the seeking love of God in person. He is the one who welcomes sinners and eats with them, embodying the father who runs down the road. In Him God is not waiting stiffly for sinners to grovel but sprinting to meet them.
basic.god: God is revealed as a seeking, running, celebrating Father, moved with compassion for the lost and full of joy when they return. He does not merely permit the sinner back; He watches the road, runs, embraces, clothes, and feasts. And He goes out to plead even with the resentful, self-righteous elder son.
basic.crossReferences: Ezekiel 34 promises that God Himself will seek His lost sheep. Luke 19 shows the Son of Man come to seek and to save the lost. Romans 5 says that while we were still sinners, Christ died for us. 1 Timothy 1 calls Paul the foremost of sinners whom Christ came to save.
basic.oneStory: Against the grumbling of the religious, Jesus unveils the joy at the center of the universe: God seeking the lost until He finds them and running to welcome them home. The story runs from a shepherd's search to a father's embrace, and it presses the question left hanging over the elder brother, will we come in and share the Father's joy?

context.literary:
Luke 15 opens with a scene and closes without a verdict. The scene is 15:1-2, where tax collectors and sinners draw near to listen and the Pharisees and scribes mutter. Luke tells us that Jesus told them 'this parable,' 15:3, in the singular, and then gives three stories that are meant to be heard as one. The singular is the key: the three panels are one argument, and the grumblers of verse 2 are the audience of every line.

The stories escalate by proportion and by price. One sheep in a hundred is lost, then one coin in ten, then one son in two. The loss grows from a small fraction to a half of the family. The search also changes. The shepherd goes out, the woman sweeps the house, and the father, who cannot search because the son has left by his own will, waits and watches until he sees him still far off. The first two stories end with a call to others, 'Rejoice with me,' 15:6 and 15:9, and a statement about heaven, 15:7 and 15:10. The third story turns that invitation into a question: will the elder brother go in?

The third story is a diptych. The first panel, 15:11-24, ends with the father's words, 'dead and is alive again... lost and is found,' and the party begins. The second, 15:25-32, ends with the same words in 15:32, now spoken to the brother who stands outside. That repeated line is an inclusio. The father's explanation for the feast is identical for both sons, and only the second hearer is left hanging, which suggests the story is addressed to a reader still deciding.

The pair of man and woman in the first two stories is also deliberate. Luke is known for placing a story about a man beside one about a woman, and the two openings, 'What man among you' and 'what woman,' draw in every hearer. The final story sets two sons on one stage. Throughout, the Pharisees' charge, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them,' is never answered in argument; it is answered by stories that show what kind of God would do so.
context.historical:
The setting is the table. The charge in 15:2 is that Jesus welcomes sinners and eats with them, and in that society sharing a meal was a sign of acceptance and shared standing. Luke has already shown the same grumbling in 5:30, and he will show it again when Jesus stays at the house of Zacchaeus, 19:7. The verb that Luke uses for the muttering in 15:2 and 19:7 belongs to those two scenes alone in the New Testament, which ties this chapter to the story where the lost man is found in a sycamore tree.

Sheep were the common wealth of a village. A shepherd with a hundred sheep owned a modest flock, and a loss of one was a real loss. The BSB gives 'pasture' in 15:4, but the Greek is the word usually used for the wilderness, which makes the ninety-nine seem more exposed and the search more costly. The woman's ten silver coins, 15:8, are drachmas, and the BSB footnote says each was worth about a day's wages. A woman with ten had the equivalent of a small reserve. A house with a small window needed a lamp even in the day, and the earthen floor had to be swept to find a lost coin.

The younger son's request in 15:12 was extraordinary. Under the law of Deuteronomy 21:17 the firstborn received a double portion, so in a two-son family the younger would inherit one third. To ask for it while the father lived was to treat him as already dead. The father granted it, and the narrative says he divided his property 'between them,' so that the elder too received his share, which makes the elder's later complaint about never being given even a young goat all the more bitter.

Feeding pigs was the lowest possible work for a Jew, since pigs were unclean under Leviticus 11:7. The son's hunger for the pods that the pigs ate marked how far he had fallen. The robe, the ring and the sandals of 15:22 are marks of honor: a ring on a finger conferred authority, as in Genesis 41:42 and Esther 8:2, and sandals were what a son wore while servants went barefoot. The fattened calf fed a whole company, which is why music and dancing could be heard from outside, 15:25. A father of standing did not run in public. The picture of him running, 15:20, was designed to be startling.
context.canonical:
The shepherd is among the oldest images of God. Psalm 23 gives it its fullest warmth, and in Psalm 119:176 a faithful man ends his prayer by saying he has gone astray like a lost sheep and asking to be sought. Isaiah 53:6 says that we all like sheep have gone astray. The great prophetic text is Ezekiel 34, where the LORD condemns the shepherds who fed themselves and promises, 'I Myself will search for My sheep,' Ezekiel 34:11. Luke 15:3-7 shows Jesus doing what Ezekiel said God would do. The parallel story in Matthew 18:12-14 is told to the disciples about the little ones, and John 10:11-16 gives the shepherd a name and a death.

The father's welcome echoes some of the tenderest lines of the prophets. In Hosea 11:1-9 God says He taught Ephraim to walk and cannot give him up, and in Jeremiah 31:20 He says that His heart yearns for the child He remembers. Jacob's fear of his brother in Genesis 32-33 ends when Esau runs to meet him, embraces him and kisses him, Genesis 33:4, and Joseph weeps on his brothers' necks, Genesis 45:14-15. The younger son who goes to a far country has a long shadow in the story of Israel, who was said to have wandered and returned, Hosea 3:5.

The elder brother stands in a line of figures who resent grace shown to others. Jonah stormed away from Nineveh and sat outside the city angry that God relented, and the book ends with God's open question to him, Jonah 4:1-2 and 4:10-11. Luke ends Jesus' parable the same way, with a father's plea and no recorded answer. Deuteronomy 21:18-21 prescribes stoning for a rebellious son, which makes the father's embrace even sharper.

The harvest of the parables is in Luke itself. Jesus will say of Zacchaeus that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost, Luke 19:10, and Paul will say that Christ Jesus came into the world to save sinners, 1 Timothy 1:15. The feast of the fattened calf looks ahead to the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:7-9.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Luke writes this chapter as an answer to a question about the character of God. The Pharisees' complaint is really a theological claim: a holy God would not eat with sinners. Jesus' three stories reply that the opposite is true, and that the God who is holy is the God who goes out. The first two stories prepare the hearers by making the point on small things, a sheep and a coin, so that when the third story arrives they are ready to hear about a father.

Luke wants the hearers to see how far God will go. The shepherd leaves the flock to find one, the woman lights a lamp, and the father runs. In each case the lost thing does nothing to be found in the first two stories, and the son's repentance in the third is notably ragged. His plan in 15:18-19 is partly hunger and partly rehearsed apology, and the father does not let him finish it. He restores the son before he can offer to be a servant.

He also wants the grumbling hearers to see themselves. The elder brother is the figure on whom the story hangs. He is dutiful, angry and outside, and he calls his brother 'this son of yours,' 15:30, while the father answers with 'this brother of yours,' 15:32. The story invites the Pharisees and scribes to receive the sinners as brothers and to enter the party. Luke does not tell us what the elder brother did, because the answer is meant to be given by those who are listening.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The parables narrate what a shepherd, a woman and a father did, and they are not instructions for how to run a flock or a household. They describe God. The behavior they commend is not that of the shepherd who leaves ninety-nine in the wilderness, which was a daring move, but the joy that follows. What the story prescribes is a response: if you are a returning son, come home; if you are an elder brother, come in.

It is important not to read the younger son's actions as a model for how to leave. The text records his sin as sin, and the pigpen as its fruit. His return is what is commended, along with the honest words of 15:21, 'I have sinned against heaven and against you.' The father's welcome describes God's character and does not make the departure harmless.

The description of the elder brother is also not a rebuke of obedience. He has served and has not disobeyed a commandment, 15:29, and the father affirms that all he has is his, 15:31. The fault is in the heart: he sees his service as a wage and his brother's return as a theft. The application for the church is to ask whether our zeal for holiness has left room for rejoicing over the lost, since the Pharisees' fault was not that they wanted holiness but that they did not want the sinners found.

debates.question: Who is the central figure of the third parable?

views.label: The father and his lavish, seeking love
views.case: The parable is bracketed by a father with two sons and turns on his running welcome and his plea to the elder; the title 'prodigal' fits the father's reckless generosity as much as the son's reckless waste. Both sons are foils to display the Father's heart, which is the answer to the grumble of verse 2.

views.label: The younger son and his repentance
views.case: The dramatic arc follows the younger son from demand to degradation to return, and the classic reading holds him up as the model of repentance coming home. His 'coming to his senses' shows what turning to God looks like.

debates.bearing: Whether we name it the father or the younger son, the point converges: repentance is coming home, and it is met by a love that runs; the Father's joy, not the sinner's worthiness, fills the scene.

debates.question: Why does the parable end with the elder brother unresolved?

views.label: A direct appeal to the grumbling Pharisees
views.case: The elder son is the mirror of the scribes and Pharisees of verse 2, dutiful yet joyless, resenting grace shown to sinners. Leaving him outside, with the father still pleading, presses the hearers to decide whether they will come in and rejoice.

views.label: A warning that self-righteousness also leaves one lost
views.case: The elder son is lost in his own way, near the father's house yet far from the father's heart, trusting his record rather than his father's love. The open ending warns that respectable religion can shut a person out of the feast as surely as wild living.

debates.bearing: Both readings turn the parable on the reader: grace exposes not only the runaway but the resentful, and the Father pleads with both to come in and share His joy.

debates.question: Is the cross absent from these parables?

views.label: Yes, and that is the point of the story
views.case: Nothing in the stories mentions a sacrifice, an offering or a mediator. The shepherd finds, the woman sweeps, and the father forgives on sight. On this reading Jesus is deliberately showing that God's welcome is not bought by a payment from the sinner, and that the grumblers' demand for qualification before acceptance misunderstands God.

views.label: No, the cost is present in the telling
views.case: Others point to what the stories assume: the father bears the loss of the estate and the shame of the running, the shepherd carries the sheep on his shoulders, and the feast is paid for by the fattened calf. Luke knows where the road leads, 9:51, and the parables of grace are told by the One who will pay for what He gives.

debates.bearing: The parables are not a full account of atonement and were never meant to be. They answer the question of what God is like, and the rest of Luke and the New Testament tell how the welcome is made right, so that the God who runs to the sinner remains just, as Romans 3:25-26 holds.

study.originalLanguages:
The first word to notice is the verb that Luke uses for the grumbling in 15:2. It is diagonguzo, a compound of the verb for muttering, and it describes a murmur that passes from one person to another through a crowd. Luke uses it in 15:2 and again in 19:7, when the crowd mutters that Jesus has gone to be the guest of a sinner. The scene is set: the sinners draw near to hear while the respectable stand off and whisper.

In 15:4 the shepherd leaves his ninety-nine 'in the pasture.' The Greek noun is the one usually rendered wilderness or desert place, and it means a thinly settled and unprotected country. The translation 'pasture' is fair, but the original makes the shepherd's choice more daring, and it recalls the places where Jesus Himself often went, Luke 5:16. The shepherd 'goes after' the lost one 'until he finds it,' and the little clause 'until' marks a search with no time limit.

The younger son's wasting in 15:13 is described by a rare adverb, asotos, 'in wild living,' and its relatives appear in Ephesians 5:18, Titus 1:6 and 1 Peter 4:4 for dissipation. The older word 'squandered' in the same verse is diaskorpizo, to scatter, and Luke uses it again in 16:1 of the manager accused of wasting his master's goods. A reader moving from chapter 15 into chapter 16 hears the same verb applied to a son and to a steward, and a quiet thread of squandered possessions connects the two stories.

The turning point in 15:17 is that he 'came to his senses,' which is literally that he came to himself. The Greek is an idiom, and it fits the son's moment of clarity better than a religious word would. In 15:15 he 'hired himself out' to a citizen; the verb is a form of kollao, to join or cling, as if the boy had attached himself to a master who would not feed him. In 15:17 and 15:19 he thinks of himself as a hired servant, misthios, a day laborer who can leave. But when the father gives orders in 15:22, the people he speaks to are douloi, slaves of the household. The father never accepts the son's proposal to be a hired man, and the contrast of terms shows it.

The kiss of 15:20 is a compound verb, katephilesen, which carries the sense of kissing warmly and repeatedly. Luke uses the same verb for the sinful woman who kissed Jesus' feet in 7:38, and for Jesus' remark in 7:45. The father's welcome and the sinner's worship in Luke 7 are described in the same word.

In 15:25 the elder son hears 'music and dancing.' The first Greek word is symphonia, from which our word symphony comes, and it appears only here in the New Testament. In 15:29 he says 'I have served you,' using douleuo, the verb for a slave's labor. The word shows how he sees himself: not as a son but as a servant keeping accounts. Finally, in 15:28 the father 'pleaded' with him, the verb parakaleo, which Luke uses for entreaty and comfort, and in 15:31 he calls him teknon, 'child,' a more tender address than the BSB's 'Son' might suggest.

typology.type: The shepherd who searches for His sheep, Ezekiel 34:11-16
typology.fulfillment: The LORD promised through Ezekiel that He Himself would search for His scattered sheep, bring them from the nations and bind up the injured. Luke 15:3-7 shows that promise lived in a shepherd with one lost sheep, and Jesus told it to people who thought the leaders of Israel had the job of shepherding. The correspondence rises in John 10:11, where the good shepherd lays down His life for the sheep, and in Hebrews 13:20, where God raised from the dead the great Shepherd of the sheep. The parable falls short of the cross, since the shepherd in the story pays only with effort, while Christ pays with His life.

typology.type: The prodigal who returns from exile, Hosea 3:5 and Jeremiah 31:18-20
typology.fulfillment: Israel in exile is spoken of as a son who has left, and the prophets promise that the child will turn and come back to a God whose heart yearns for him. The younger son's journey to a far country and his return are the pattern of Israel's story in miniature. In Christ the return is no longer only national: those who were far off are brought near, Ephesians 2:13, and the whole company of the lost is gathered. The type falls short in that the son in the story returns by his own resolve, while the New Testament says that God's grace begins the turning, Romans 2:4.

typology.type: The covering of shame, robe and ring
typology.fulfillment: The best robe given to the returned son recalls God's clothing of Adam and Eve in Genesis 3:21, and the prophets use clothing to speak of forgiveness, as in Zechariah 3:3-5, where Joshua's filthy garments are removed and rich ones put on. In Christ the correspondence becomes an exchange: believers are clothed with Christ, Galatians 3:27, and given the robe of righteousness, Isaiah 61:10. The type falls short because the robe in the parable is simply given, with no account of how the cost was met.

The feasts of Israel were meant to be joyful meals before the LORD in the land he gave, Deuteronomy 16:11. The father's feast for a son who was dead and alive again is a picture of the joy of heaven, 15:7 and 15:10, and it points to the table of the kingdom. In Christ it is the Lord's Supper and the wedding supper of the Lamb, Revelation 19:9. The type is partial because the feast in the story is for one household, while the Lamb's supper gathers people from every nation, Revelation 7:9.

study.christ:
The chapter leads to Christ first because it begins with Him. The Pharisees' complaint, 'This man welcomes sinners and eats with them,' is an accurate description of Jesus' ministry, and the three parables are His defense of it. When He eats with tax collectors, He is not lowering His standards; He is acting out the character of God. Jesus is therefore not only the teller of the stories but their living illustration. The shepherd in the first parable is a figure for God, and Ezekiel had promised that God Himself would shepherd His flock, so when Jesus does it, the claim is large.

He is the one who seeks. Luke 19:10 gives the plainest summary: the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. The three parables are told in the middle of a journey toward Jerusalem, and the journey is the searching. The chapter is also the middle of a Gospel that begins with the announcement that a Savior is born, 2:11, and ends with a risen Lord who sends repentance and forgiveness to all nations, 24:47. The shepherd's carrying of the sheep on his shoulders is a picture that John 10:11 will turn into a death and 1 Peter 2:25 will turn into a return, since those who were straying like sheep have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls.

He is the answer to the elder brother's complaint as well. The elder son resents that sinners are received at the family table, and the Man who tells the story is the one who sits at that table with them. Hebrews 2:11 says that He is not ashamed to call those He saves His brothers. The grumbling Pharisees are being shown what the real family resemblance looks like.

The cost of the feast is also His. The father pays in the loss of his estate and the loss of his dignity, but the New Testament says that the welcome of God is made right at a cross. In Romans 3:25-26 God presented Christ as a sacrifice so that He might be just and the one who justifies those who have faith. Luke does not state this in chapter 15, and the reading should be careful not to import the cross into the robe, the ring and the calf as though each were a code. The correct claim is that the Man who tells these stories is the one who will bear the cost of what He describes.

Guard against allegory also keeps the reading honest. The coin, the ring and the sandals do not each represent a doctrine. The center is Jesus' answer to those who said He should not eat with sinners: this is what God is like, and this is why I am here.
study.god:
Luke 15 gives the most direct portrait of God in the Gospels. The first thing it shows is that God takes the initiative. The shepherd leaves the ninety-nine, the woman lights the lamp, and the father scans the road. The lost do nothing to be sought. The God of this chapter is not waiting to see whether sinners will clean themselves up; He goes out and brings them in.

He is a God of feeling. The father is 'filled with compassion,' 15:20, and the joy of heaven, mentioned in 15:7 and 15:10, is a real joy. This answers the picture of God as a stern accountant. The theology of the chapter says that God is glad. It also says that He is the kind of God whose gladness is shared: the shepherd and the woman call their friends, and the father throws a feast. God's joy is not private. It invites others in.

He is a God who honors the freedom of the sinner. The father does not stop the younger son from leaving and does not follow him. He lets the boy have what he asks for. This is not indifference, as the watching on the road shows, but it means that God's love does not coerce. At the same time it is a love that does not need to be earned: the father interrupts the confession, and the best robe is put on before the son can offer to be a servant.

He is a God who pleads. The father goes out to the elder son, who is angry and outside, and says 'Son, you are always with me, and all that is mine is yours.' The same love that runs to the sinner goes out to the self-righteous. It is worth noticing that the father addresses both sons with tenderness, and that the elder's complaint is met with an explanation and not a rebuke.

He is just as well as merciful. The younger son's words, 'I have sinned against heaven and against you,' name sin as an offense against God. The parable does not treat the waste as trivial, and the pigpen is a real consequence. But the way the story ends shows that the final word is not judgment but restoration, and the New Testament tells how justice and mercy meet at the cross, Romans 3:25-26.

For worship, the chapter says that we should rejoice in what God rejoices in. A congregation that is grudging about the return of the lost has not yet understood the God it worships. The right response to this God is to come home if we are far away, and to come in if we are standing outside the door with our arms folded.

crossReferences.note: The LORD says He will search for His sheep, seek them out, rescue them from every place where they were scattered, and bind up the injured. This is the promise behind the shepherd of Luke 15:4-7, and it explains why Jesus' search for the lost is a claim about who He is.

A faithful man ends his long prayer by saying he has strayed like a lost sheep and asking God to seek his servant. Even the devout in Israel could see themselves as sheep in need of finding, which sets a gentle limit on the ninety-nine who 'do not need to repent' in Luke 15:7.

God remembers teaching Ephraim to walk and says His heart recoils within Him and His compassion grows warm. The language of a father's torn feelings for a wandering child stands behind the father who is filled with compassion in Luke 15:20.

Esau runs to meet Jacob, embraces him, falls on his neck and kisses him, though Jacob had feared revenge. The pattern of a wronged brother who runs to the one who deserved judgment appears again in the father's run in Luke 15:20.

The firstborn is to receive a double portion of the inheritance. This is the background for the younger son's share in Luke 15:12 and for the elder's complaint in 15:29-31, since the father's last words to him remind him that everything that remains is his.

Jonah is angry that God spared Nineveh, and the book ends with God's question about whether He should not care for that great city. The open ending matches Luke 15:32: both stories leave a resentful man outside while the one he resents is shown mercy.

Levi throws a banquet and the Pharisees complain that Jesus eats with tax collectors and sinners. Jesus answers that He has not come to call the righteous but sinners to repentance. The grumbling of Luke 15:2 is the same objection, and the three parables are the longer answer.

At Zacchaeus' house the crowd again mutters that Jesus has gone to be the guest of a sinner, and He ends with the declaration that the Son of Man came to seek and to save the lost. It is the real-life case of what the parables describe.

Peter says that believers were going astray like sheep but have now returned to the Shepherd and Overseer of their souls. The sheep who is found and carried home in Luke 15:5 becomes the picture of every Christian's story.

God put forward Christ as a propitiation, so that He might be both just and the justifier of the one who has faith in Jesus. It states what Luke 15 leaves untold: how the father who forgives remains righteous in welcoming those who deserve judgment.

study.oneStory:
The Bible's story begins with a Father who gives everything to His children, and the first sin is the first departure. In Genesis 3 the man and woman leave the garden under judgment, and the story moves east, away from the presence. The younger son in Luke 15 is the whole human story in one boy: he receives good gifts, takes them away from the giver, spends them, and ends hungry among pigs. The question the rest of Scripture asks is whether anyone will go after those who have gone.

The Old Testament answers with promises. Moses interceded for a people who had gone astray at the mountain, Exodus 32. The prophets said that the LORD would shepherd His scattered flock, Ezekiel 34, and that He would bring Ephraim home, Jeremiah 31:20. Exile was the far country of Israel, and the return was the hope. But the story also shows an elder brother in Israel, Jonah and the prophets' rivals, who resented mercy for the nations.

Luke 15 is where the promise appears in the form of a person. Jesus eats with sinners because that is what the Shepherd does, and the Father's heart is revealed in His behavior. The parables explain why He came, as Luke 19:10 says, and the road ahead goes to a cross where the cost of the seeking is paid. The resurrection is then the father's cry made real: this one was dead and is alive again. In Acts the story goes on, with the gospel running to Samaria and to the nations, and with the same grumbling in the mouths of those who cannot believe that God would accept the Gentiles, Acts 11:1-18.

The story ends in a feast. The wedding supper of the Lamb is the party at which the lost are found, and the joy of heaven becomes the joy of a whole people from every nation, Revelation 7:9 and 19:9. The elder brother's question remains open until the end of the age, because a story of grace cannot compel anyone to come in, but it can plead.

In the new creation the tears of the far country are wiped away, Revelation 21:4. Every lost sheep and coin and son who has been found is gathered in one house, and the house is the Father's, where God Himself dwells with His people, Revelation 21:3. Those who are there will not have earned the place. They will be there because they were sought, and they will be glad.

quiz.q: Why does Jesus tell these three parables?

options.text: To answer the Pharisees and scribes who grumbled that He welcomes sinners and eats with them.
options.note: Luke 15:1-3 sets the parables as a direct reply to the grumbling.

options.text: To teach that God cares about lost and forgotten things.
options.note: True in substance, but the specific occasion is the objection to His welcoming sinners.

options.text: To encourage shepherds and housekeepers in their daily work.
options.note: The everyday images serve a deeper point about God's joy over repentant sinners.

options.text: To warn sinners to stay away from Him.
options.note: The opposite: He welcomes sinners, and heaven rejoices when they come.

quiz.q: What does heaven do when one sinner repents?

options.text: Heaven rejoices, and there is joy in the presence of God's angels.
options.note: Luke 15:7,10 declares joy in heaven over one sinner who repents.

options.text: God notes the sinner's return with approval.
options.note: True but understated; Scripture speaks not of quiet approval but of overflowing joy.

options.text: The angels record the repentance for the day of judgment.
options.note: The text speaks of present rejoicing, not merely record-keeping.

options.text: Heaven remains unmoved unless many repent at once.
options.note: The joy is expressly over one sinner who repents.

quiz.q: How does the father respond when the younger son returns?

options.text: While the son is still far off, the father is filled with compassion, runs to him, embraces him, and throws a feast.
options.note: Luke 15:20-24 shows the running, compassionate welcome and celebration.

options.text: The father forgives the son and restores him to the family.
options.note: True, but it misses the striking picture of the father running while the son is still far off.

options.text: The father waits for the son to finish his prepared apology first.
options.note: The father runs and embraces him before the son can finish; the welcome precedes the full speech.

options.text: The father makes the son work as a hired servant to earn his place.
options.note: The son is restored as a son with robe, ring, and feast, not demoted to a servant.

quiz.q: What is the point of the elder brother in the third parable?

options.text: He mirrors the grumbling religious leaders, dutiful yet joyless, resenting grace shown to sinners.
options.note: The elder son embodies the Pharisees of verse 2 who resent Jesus welcoming sinners.

options.text: He shows that self-righteousness can leave a person outside the feast.
options.note: True, but it does not name the pointed link to the grumbling leaders Jesus is addressing.

options.text: He teaches that hard work should be rewarded.
options.note: The parable exposes his resentment, not a lesson about rewarding diligence.

options.text: He proves the younger son should not have been forgiven.
options.note: The father defends the celebration; the elder son's complaint is gently corrected.

quiz.q: What does the repeated phrase 'lost and found' reveal about God?

options.text: God actively seeks the lost until He finds them and rejoices to restore them to life.
options.note: The shepherd, the woman, and the father all seek and rejoice, revealing the seeking God.

options.text: God is willing to receive those who find their own way back.
options.note: Partly true of the son, but the sheep and coin are sought and found by another, stressing God's initiative.

options.text: God keeps careful count of who is missing.
options.note: The counting serves the deeper truth of a God who searches and rejoices, not mere bookkeeping.

options.text: God leaves the lost to return entirely on their own.
options.note: The shepherd goes after the sheep and the father runs; God takes the initiative.

questions: The shepherd went after the one until he found it. Where do you need to know that God has been seeking you, not waiting for you to find your own way back?
The father ran while his son was still a long way off. Does your picture of God match this, a Father sprinting to meet returning sinners, or do you imagine Him reluctant and cold?
The younger son rehearsed a speech about becoming a servant, but the father restored him as a son. Are you trying to earn back a place that grace wants to give you freely?
The elder brother kept the rules yet missed the father's heart and stood outside the party. Where might dutiful religion be leaving you resentful of the grace God shows to others?
Heaven throws a party over one sinner who repents. Whose repentance could you celebrate this week, and does the joy of God shape how you treat people who come home?

translationNotes.note: The ten silver coins are Greek drachmas, each worth about a day's wages; the single lost coin may have been part of a woman's savings or dowry, which explains the diligent, lamp-lit search.

Some manuscripts add to the son's confession the line 'Make me like one of your hired servants' from his rehearsed speech in verse 19; the father cuts the speech short with restoration before the son can finish.

'Was dead and is alive again, was lost and is found' is the refrain of the whole chapter. Being lost is pictured as a kind of death, and being found as resurrection, language that reaches its fullness in the gospel of Christ.
